gallery.filename: Chingkhei Eekon - a sacred pond of the Meitei people in the northeastern corner of the citadel and the palace building of the Kangla fort in Imphal.jpg
gallery.title: File:Chingkhei Eekon - a sacred pond of the Meitei people in the northeastern corner of the citadel and the palace building of the Kangla fort in Imphal.jpg
gallery.source: Chingkhei Eekon - a sacred pond of the Meitei people in the northeastern corner of the citadel and the palace building of the Kangla fort in Imphal
gallery.description: Chingkhei Eekon is a sacred pond of the Meitei people in the northeastern corner of the citadel and the palace building of the Kangla fort in Imphal. In Meitei language (officially called Manipuri language), "Chingkhei" means "Northeast" and "Eekon" means "Pond". Chingkhei Eekon is also called Chingkhei Pukhri, Chingkhei Ekon or Chingkhei Ikon.

gallery.filename: Manung Thangapat - the Inner Moat of the Kangla Fort in Imphal.jpg
gallery.title: File:Manung Thangapat - the Inner Moat of the Kangla Fort in Imphal.jpg
gallery.source: Manung Thangapat - the Inner Moat of the Kangla Fort in Imphal
gallery.description: Manung Thangapat is the Inner Moat of the Kangla Fort in Imphal. It protects the Kangla Palace as a second line of defense. Inside its encircled region, there lies the citadel of the Kangla fort. In Meitei language (officially known as Manipuri language), "Manung" means "Inner" and "Thangapat" means "Moat".

gallery.filename: Manung Kangjeibung - the Polo Ground of the Meitei royalties, located inside the Kangla fort in Imphal.jpg
gallery.title: File:Manung Kangjeibung - the Polo Ground of the Meitei royalties, located inside the Kangla fort in Imphal.jpg
gallery.source: Manung Kangjeibung - the Polo Ground of the Meitei royalties, located inside the Kangla fort in Imphal
gallery.description:
Manung Kangjeibung is the Polo Ground of the Meitei royalties, located inside the Kangla fort in Imphal, the capital city of Kangleipak (Manipur). It was developed for the first time during the time of King Ningthou Kangba (1405 BC – 1359 BC) and later re-developed during the reign of King Ningthou Marjit Singh (1813 AD – 1819 AD). In Meitei language (Manipuri language), "Manung" means "inner" and "Kangjeibung" means "polo ground". 
Presently, this historic polo ground is also serving as a helipad.

gallery.filename: Northern view of the classical colossal statues of Kanglasha, the Meitei mythical Dragon Lion God, located inside the Kangla Fort in Imphal.jpg
gallery.title: File:Northern view of the classical colossal statues of Kanglasha, the Meitei mythical Dragon Lion God, located inside the Kangla Fort in Imphal.jpg
gallery.source: Northern view of the classical colossal statues of Kanglasha, the Meitei mythical Dragon Lion God, located inside the Kangla Fort in Imphal
gallery.description: The image shows the northern view of the Statues of Kanglasha, the Meitei mythical Dragon Lion God, located inside the Kangla Fort in Imphal. Kanglasha is a single individual but his sculptures are usually displayed either in dual (2) or quadruple (4). These statues are meant for protection of the royalties from the evil spirits. These are made up of bricks and mortars. After getting destroyed by the British Army during the annexation of the Kangla fort, as a result of the Anglo-Manipuri war in 1891, these two structures were rebuilt and repaired by the Government of Manipur after getting independence from the British Empire. In Meitei language (officially known as Manipuri language), "Kanglasha" means "Beast of the Kangla". Kanglasha is also known as Nongshaba (literally, " The Male Lion" in Meitei language).

gallery.description: The image shows the southern gateway to the citadel of the Kangla fort in Imphal. It leads to the ruins of the Sanggai Yumpham (Royal Residence) of the Meitei royalties of Kangleipak kingdom (Manipur kingdom).

gallery.filename: Southwestern view of the Kangla Uttra Shanglen, the religious office building of Sanamahism, inside the Kangla fort in Imphal.jpg
gallery.title: File:Southwestern view of the Kangla Uttra Shanglen, the religious office building of Sanamahism, inside the Kangla fort in Imphal.jpg
gallery.source: Southwestern view of the Kangla Uttra Shanglen, the religious office building of Sanamahism, inside the Kangla fort in Imphal
gallery.description: The image shows the southwestern view of Kangla Uttra Shanglen (AKA "Uttra Sanglen"), the religious office building of Sanamahism (traditional Meitei religion), located inside the Kangla Fort in Imphal. It is built in the traditional Meitei architectural designs, among which the most significant and the holiest element is the "chirong" (literally, "horns" in Meitei language) which is the V-shaped design adorned on the roof of the building.

gallery.description: A tree of Koubilla (Grevillea robusta) species growing inside the Kangla fort in Imphal, Kangleipak (Manipur). Koubilla is a Meitei language name of the Silky Oak (Grevillea robusta A.Cunn. ex R.Br.) species.

gallery.title: File:Statue of Maharaja Nara Singh in front of the Western Entrance to the Kangla fort in Imphal.jpg
gallery.source: Statue of Maharaja Nara Singh in front of the Western Entrance to the Kangla fort in Imphal
gallery.description: The image shows the statue of Maharaja Nara Singh in front of the Western Entrance to the Kangla fort in Imphal. Maharaja Nara Singh (AKA Meidingu Narasingh) was a Meitei monarch of the Ningthouja dynasty, who ruled Kangleipak kingdom (Manipur kingdom) in the 19th century AD.

gallery.filename: The Manglen of Maharaja Bodhchandra inside the Kangla Fort in Imphal.jpg
gallery.title: File:The Manglen of Maharaja Bodhchandra inside the Kangla Fort in Imphal.jpg
gallery.source: The Manglen of Maharaja Bodhchandra inside the Kangla Fort in Imphal
gallery.description: The image shows the Manglen of Maharaja Bodhchandra inside the Kangla fort in Imphal. "Manglen" is the site where kings of Kangleipak (Manipur) were cremated. The mortal remains of Maharaja Bodhchandra Singh (Bodhachandra Singh), the last ruler of sovereign state of Manipur, was consigned to flames at this place on the 9th December, 1955.
